BBC live, 23 Nov (evening retrieval)

Andy Burnham says it's \"unthinkable\" that the UK would rejoin the EU without a referendum - he's currently facing questions from his MPs about his new UK-EU deal

He says \"too many bridges were burned with Europe\" during the first Brexit deal, and Britain should consider a \"range of options\" going forward

The new deal includes a youth mobility scheme, scrapping most checks on British food exports, and the linking of EU and UK emissions trading systems - see a recap here

It's not a surprise that Andy Burnham said it would be \"unthinkable\" to take the UK back into the EU without a referendum, writes our political correspondent

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch says reopening the Brexit debate is \"the last thing our country needs\"

Burnham earlier said he would ignore \"stuck in the past\" former prime ministers who have criticised his approach to the EU - what have they said?

We can now bring you some more lines from the CBI conference in London, where party leaders have been addressing business delegates.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski puts forward a case for rejoining the EU.

\"I think whether you look from a business point of view, from a cultural point of view and also from a national security point of view, we are much better being part of this bloc,\" he says.

Polanski goes on to criticise Labour for not going far enough and saying \"different things to different audiences\".

Polanski puts forward a case for rejoining EU

By policy and analysis correspondent Ben Chu

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the House of Commons the UK-EU deal would take “pressure off the cost of the weekly shop”.

However, the Fresh Produce Consortium (FPC) has said the deal risks putting upward pressure on UK food prices rather than reducing them.

The FPC has previously warned the deal would require the UK government to bring in EU-aligned import requirements on produce from the rest of the world which at the moment mainly don’t apply.

The FPC estimates these new checks - aimed at stopping potentially unsafe food getting into the EU via the UK - could add £300m a year of extra costs which it says might be passed on to shoppers.

It also notes that since Brexit, the UK has not imposed import checks on fresh fruit and vegetable items from the EU - which might mean the deal can’t deliver significant savings for these products.

One area though where there could be potential savings are for imports of some EU products the UK has imposed checks on, like meat. The prices of these food imports from the EU could still potentially come down.

The overall impact on UK food prices of the UK-EU deal will depend on how these different effects balance out, and how much of any additional costs or savings businesses pass on to consumers.

Will the EU deal raise or lower UK food prices?

The prime minister has just set out his UK-EU deal to MPs in the Commons, which includes a youth mobility scheme and scrapping most checks on British food exports.

In response, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch described it as \"foolish\" to \"tell everyone how desperate you are\" when negotiating a deal, which she said was what Burnham had done.

Instead of focusing on lowering the cost of living, she said Burnham treated the opportunity as a \"political performance\", and that the deal would see the UK becoming a \"rule-taker from Brussels\".

She added that the deal would make energy bills in the UK more expensive, and accused the PM of overselling the deal \"at every level\".

Recap: Burnham hails UK-EU deal as 'landmark moment' in Commons

It’s not a surprise that Andy Burnham said it would be \"unthinkable\" to take the UK back into the EU without a referendum.

The prime minister has chosen to reopen the conversation about what the UK’s long-term future with the EU looks like.

While the process surrounding that is far from certain, Burnham has made clear in recent weeks that a full rejoining could only happen after another public vote.

We do not know whether he thinks an option short of full rejoin – such as the single market – would need a referendum too.

What’s been striking over the last couple of hours is how keen Burnham has been to turn the conversation back to the deal he signed on Friday, rather than the longer-term question.

He’s been happy to talk about food standards, emissions and youth mobility, but less so about the customs union, the single market and free movement.

More on that is coming next month in Burnham’s 10-year plan, but the PM isn’t promising full details until next year’s UK-EU summit.

For now he insisted: “There will be no banging on about Europe from this side, or a running commentary.”

Burnham's comments on EU referendum come as no surprise

Green MP Ellie Chowns welcomes the shift in tone from Labour in regards to Brexit, including steps taken by the government last week to secure a new agreement with the EU.

She asks Burnham when he'll set out the \"pathway to the truly brightest future for Britain, i.e. to rejoin the EU\".

Burnham says he'll be setting a \"bold plan for Britain next month, so she doesn't have to wait too long\".

The plan will outline how the government plans to re-industrialise Britain, give young people a new education system and encourage growth in every postcode, he says.

The PM adds that as part of it, \"we will consider what is the right long-term relationship for Britain with its largest market and nearest neighbour\".

'Truly brightest future' for Britain would be to 'rejoin the EU' - Green MP

Reform UK MP Richard Tice criticises the new UK-EU deal for increasing immigration to the UK by 300,000 under-31-year-olds, taking away opportunities from young Britons not in education, employment or training.

Tice says Burnham is treating his constituents \"like fools\", after he told Makerfield voters during the by-election that he wouldn't be re-opening the Brexit debate.

In response, Burnham says even Reform's leader Nigel Farage said Brexit has failed, pointing to Farage's criticism of the deal the Tories negotiated.

Reform criticises youth experience scheme for increasing immigration

Conservative MP Sir Bernard Jenkin asks the PM to give a \"clear unequivocal statement that it would be unthinkable for any prime minister to try and take the UK back into the EU without a referendum\".

Burnham replies: \"Yes it would be unthinkable.\"

'It would be unthinkable' to rejoin EU without referendum - Burnham

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves congratulates Burnham on the deal he secured for Britain last week.

\"I'm proud to have been the first chancellor in more than a decade who's sought to strengthen rather than sever our relations with the European Union,\" she tells the House of Commons.

She asks: \"Will the prime minister agree with me that the best way to build on the very strong growth and productivity numbers that we've achieved in the last two years, is to continue to strengthen both our security and economic relations with our nearest neighbours and trading partners?\"

Burnham responds by saying he agrees strongly with Reeves, paying tribute to her in her role as chancellor, and to the former PM, Keir Starmer, in \"laying the ground\" for the agreement that has been reached.

They were both acting in the best interests of the country, he says, enabling a new agreement that will boost Britain's security, economy and exports.

Reeves among Labour MPs congratulating Burnham on deal

Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey welcomes the new deal's youth mobility scheme, food export agreement, and linking the emissions market, saying those elements should have been part of the original Brexit deal.

Davey asks whether Burnham stands by that description, and if not will he replace the \"failed\" agreement and get a new deal for Britain?

Burnham responds by saying the new deal \"takes steps to improve it\" and the government will continue to look at options for the \"long-term relationship\" between the UK and EU.

\"Let me stand here and say unequivocally I believe in the deal we have negotiated,\" he says.

\"I think it is good for Britain, it is in our national interest. The House should support it.\"

Lib Dems leader welcomes new EU deal to replace 'failed' Tory agreement

Burnham responds to Badenoch by saying the Conservatives used to back British businesses but are now happy to saddle them with \"mountains of red tape\".

He says the Tories took the UK out of the EU without a plan for growth, and the Labour government now has to deal with the reality of that situation.

This deal will add to British growth in the years ahead, he says, calling Labour the \"pro-growth party\".

Responding to criticism that the Brexit debate shouldn't be reopened, Burnham points out that the Tories want to take the UK out of the European Court of Human Rights, which would also mean having to re-negotiate elements of the Brexit deal.

\"They need to get clear about what their party policy actually is,\" he says, as he criticises the party opposite for \"mistakes that damaged Britain and left us where we are today\".

Burnham condemns Tories for Brexit 'mistakes that damaged Britain'

Badenoch goes on to say the prime minister has oversold the UK-EU deal \"at every level\", accusing Burnham of \"selectively\" quoting organisations.

She says the deal will make energy bills more expensive, and make it more difficult to bring them down in the long term.

Badenoch moves on to criticise the youth experience scheme, pointing out that Burnham's predecessor Keir Starmer wanted no more than 30,000 young people coming to the UK from the EU, while Burnham has agreed to \"up to 300,000 over three years\".

British young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) will have to compete with Europeans \"for the few jobs Labour hasn't managed to kill yet\", she says.

Badenoch highlights how a number of former prime ministers have criticised reopening the Brexit debate, accusing Burnham of \"living in the past\" and \"trying to take Britain back to 2015 instead of focusing on the future\".

PM has oversold the UK-EU deal 'at every level' - Badenoch

Responding to the prime minister's statement, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch says it is \"spectacularly foolish\" when negotiating  to \"tell everyone how desperate you are\".

\"Of course he didn't get a good deal, because when Labour negotiate, Britain loses,\" says Badenoch.

She says this deal is not about \"reducing the cost of living\", but that the prime minister has instead treated it as a \"political performance\".

Burnham, Badenoch says, has committed the UK to becoming a \"rule-taker from Brussels\", something she says he has no mandate to do.
